--- title: "MA388 Sabermetrics: Lesson 32" subtitle: "Linear Weights" author: "LTC Jim Pleuss" format: html: theme: cosmo toc: true pdf: documentclass: article execute: echo: true warning: false message: false --- # Lesson Objectives 1. Derive linear weights for singles, doubles, triples, home runs, walks, and outs from run-value data. 2. Compute Batting Runs for each player using Thorn and Palmer's linear weights model. 3. Compare Batting Runs to traditional statistics (AVG, SLG, OPS, RBI) and assess which better measures offensive contribution. 4. Convert Batting Runs to wins using the 10-runs-per-win rule of thumb. ## Review **What characteristics of a hitter does OPS quantify?** \vspace{1.in} **Why might one use OPS+ or adjusted OPS+ instead of OPS?** \vspace{1.in} **What are some limitations of these statistics?** \vspace{1.in} ## Linear Weights **Recall we talked about the relationship between Runs and Wins in Chapter 4 of the Albert text. What was the rule of thumb we used?** \vspace{1.in} (*Understanding Sabermetrics* page 136) Ideally, we want a statistic for batters that: - quantifies their contribution to runs scored. - is not based upon the situations the batters faced when they came to the plate (since their batting actions did not create those situations). **How about RBIs? A batter is awarded Runs Batted In (RBIs) for most situations when his plate appearance results in runs scored. Why are RBIs not a good measure of a player’s contribution to runs scored?** \vspace{1.in} Various researchers have proposed linear models to quantify a player’s contribution to runs scored. These models give weights to various individual statistics. For the purposes of today’s lesson, let’s investigate the condensed model proposed by Thorn and Palmer (*Understanding Sabermetrics*, page 143). I’ll refer to this model as the Linear Weights Model: $$BattingRuns = w_11B + w_22B + w_33B + w_4HR + w_5(BB + HBP) - w_6(AB - H)$$ How can we get weights for the Linear Weights Model? \vspace{1.in} ::: {.html}
::: $$RV = EXP_{New} - EXP_{Old} + RunsScored$$ How do we interpret BattingRuns? \vspace{1.in} ::: {.html}
::: Let’s see what this looks like for the 2011 season. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(Lahman) library(tidyverse) library(plotly) library(knitr) # Calculate weights from run values using Retrosheet play-by-play data. # We're getting this file from GitHub in the linear_weights() function, # but you can adapt it to a Retrosheet file you have locally if desired. source("linear_weights.R") weights <- linear_weights(2011) |> pluck("weights") weights |> kable(digits = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Event | weight| |:------|------:| |1B | 0.442| |2B | 0.736| |3B | 1.064| |BB.HBP | 0.289| |HR | 1.392| |Out | -0.255| ::: ::: How do these weights compare to those in slugging percentage (SLG)? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Filter for 2011 Players with at least 500 at-bats. vars = c("AB", "H", "X2B", "X3B", "HR", "BB", "HBP", "SF", "RBI") Batting |> filter(yearID == 2011) |> group_by(playerID,teamID) |> summarise_at(vars, sum) |> ungroup() |> filter(AB >= 500) |> left_join(People |> select(nameLast, nameFirst, playerID) )|> mutate(name = paste(nameFirst, nameLast, sep = " "))|> select(name, everything(), -nameLast, -nameFirst) |> mutate(X1B = H - X2B - X3B -HR, SLG = (X1B + 2*X2B + 3*X3B + 4*HR) / AB, OBP = (H + HBP + BB) / (AB + HBP + SF + BB), OPS = SLG + OBP, AVG = H / AB) -> batting_2011 # Calculates Batting Runs using Thorn and Palmer's condensed Linear Weights model. # Note: Statistics and weights have to be in the same order. batting_runs_fn <- function(statistics, weights){ runs <- round(sum(statistics * weights), 1) return(runs) } batting_2011 |> group_by(playerID) |> mutate(batting_runs = batting_runs_fn(statistics = c(X1B, X2B, X3B, BB + HBP, HR, AB - H), weights = weights |> pull(weight))) |> ungroup() |> arrange(-batting_runs) -> batting_2011 batting_2011 |> select(name, AB, H, HR, RBI, AVG, OPS, batting_runs) |> head(10) |> kable(digits = 3, caption = "Top 10 MLB Players (with at least 500 at bats) - Batting Runs 2011") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Top 10 MLB Players (with at least 500 at bats) - Batting Runs 2011 |name | AB| H| HR| RBI| AVG| OPS| batting_runs| |:-----------------|---:|---:|--:|---:|-----:|-----:|------------:| |Jose Bautista | 513| 155| 43| 103| 0.302| 1.056| 66.4| |Miguel Cabrera | 572| 197| 30| 105| 0.344| 1.033| 66.3| |Matt Kemp | 602| 195| 39| 126| 0.324| 0.986| 54.9| |Prince Fielder | 569| 170| 38| 120| 0.299| 0.981| 54.7| |Adrian Gonzalez | 630| 213| 27| 117| 0.338| 0.957| 51.9| |Ryan Braun | 563| 187| 33| 111| 0.332| 0.994| 51.4| |Joey Votto | 599| 185| 29| 103| 0.309| 0.947| 50.5| |Jacoby Ellsbury | 660| 212| 32| 105| 0.321| 0.928| 44.3| |David Ortiz | 525| 162| 29| 96| 0.309| 0.953| 41.9| |Curtis Granderson | 583| 153| 41| 119| 0.262| 0.916| 39.0| ::: ::: **How many wins would you attribute to Prince Fielder in the 2011 season?** \vspace{1.in} ::: {.html}
::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} batting_2011 |> select(name, AB, H, HR, RBI, AVG, OPS, batting_runs) |> tail(10) |> kable(digits = 3, caption = "Bottom 10 MLB Players (with at least 500 at bats) - Batting Runs 2011") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Bottom 10 MLB Players (with at least 500 at bats) - Batting Runs 2011 |name | AB| H| HR| RBI| AVG| OPS| batting_runs| |:-------------------|---:|---:|--:|---:|-----:|-----:|------------:| |Juan Pierre | 639| 178| 2| 50| 0.279| 0.657| -14.8| |Vernon Wells | 505| 110| 25| 66| 0.218| 0.660| -15.2| |Ian Desmond | 584| 148| 8| 49| 0.253| 0.656| -15.7| |Yuniesky Betancourt | 556| 140| 13| 68| 0.252| 0.652| -16.7| |Alcides Escobar | 548| 139| 4| 46| 0.254| 0.633| -19.4| |Alex Gonzalez | 564| 136| 15| 56| 0.241| 0.642| -19.4| |Ichiro Suzuki | 677| 184| 5| 47| 0.272| 0.645| -19.8| |Casey McGehee | 546| 122| 13| 67| 0.223| 0.626| -20.1| |Jason Bartlett | 554| 136| 2| 40| 0.245| 0.615| -20.8| |Alex Rios | 537| 122| 13| 44| 0.227| 0.613| -23.3| ::: ::: What happens if you total up all the batting runs in a season? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} batting_2011 |> summarize(tot_batting_runs=sum(batting_runs),.by='teamID') |> arrange(-tot_batting_runs) |> left_join(Teams |> filter(yearID==2011) |> select(teamID,actual_wins=W), by = 'teamID') |> head(10) |> kable(digits = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |teamID | tot_batting_runs| actual_wins| |:------|----------------:|-----------:| |BOS | 162.0| 90| |NYA | 116.7| 97| |DET | 99.0| 95| |TOR | 78.3| 81| |CIN | 76.0| 79| |KCA | 74.9| 71| |MIL | 69.3| 96| |LAN | 59.6| 82| |BAL | 48.5| 69| |TEX | 48.2| 96| ::: ::: Let’s see how BattingRuns compares to traditional statistics. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(gridExtra) title_size = 12 plot_rbi <- batting_2011 |> ggplot(aes(label = name, x = batting_runs, y = RBI)) + geom_point() + labs(title = "Linear Weights vs. RBI") + theme_classic() + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = title_size)) plot_avg <- batting_2011 |> ggplot(aes(label = name, x = batting_runs, y = AVG)) + geom_point() + labs(title = "Linear Weights vs. Batting Average") + theme_classic() + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = title_size)) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_slg <- batting_2011 |> ggplot(aes(label = name, x = batting_runs, y = SLG)) + geom_point() + labs(title = "Linear Weights vs. Slugging") + theme_classic() + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = title_size)) plot_ops <- batting_2011 |> ggplot(aes(label = name, x = batting_runs, y = OPS)) + geom_point() + labs(title = "Linear Weights vs. OPS") + theme_classic() + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = title_size)) grid.arrange(plot_rbi, plot_avg, plot_slg, plot_ops, ncol = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lsn_32_linear_weights_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-6-1.pdf){fig-pos='H'} ::: ::: Let’s say you’re a general manager. Which statistic would you use? \vspace{1.in} ::: {.html}
::: What other factors would you want to consider? \vspace{1.in} ::: {.html}
::: In terms of BattingRuns, is it more important to hit for power or on base percentage? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} batting_2011 |> ungroup() |> # Before adding this, scale() returned NaN for everything. mutate(OBP_scaled = scale(OBP), SLG_scaled = scale(SLG), BR_scaled = scale(batting_runs)) |> ggplot(aes(x = OBP_scaled, y = SLG_scaled, color = BR_scaled)) + geom_point() + scale_color_viridis_b() + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lsn_32_linear_weights_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-7-1.pdf){fig-pos='H'} ::: :::
